note: Batch 1 broad family survey: raw momentum reversal volatility range beta correlation and higher moments across lookbacks to map sign and magnitude of each canonical family
Batch 2 lookback grid refinement of the four families that led batch 1: low volatility, kurtosis, intermediate momentum with short-term reversal skip, and rolling max range position
Batch 3 tests skip-window variants of intermediate momentum, volatility-scaled momentum, and cross-sectionally standardised composites of momentum plus low-vol plus kurtosis
Batch 4 upgrades each composite leg to its best lookback and compares rank-based versus z-score-based aggregation for outlier robustness
Batch 5 maps the lagged-return surface around delay ret 20 by 10 and rebuilds the multi-factor composites using it as the momentum leg

text: Approach: map canonical factor families first, then refine lookbacks, then composite. Batch 1-2 showed intermediate momentum (40-60d), low volatility (long lookback), short-window kurtosis and 60d range position all carry positive train Sharpe, while very short returns mean-revert. Batch 3-5 found the strongest primitive is a LAGGED return: delay(ret(20),10), i.e. the cumulative return from roughly t-30 to t-10, SR 2.13 IC 0.0139. The delay surface is smooth and peaks over a broad plateau (windows 10-20, lags 10-15), which is reassuring rather than a knife-edge overfit. Short-horizon returns (last 5-10 days) are the mean-reverting part, so subtracting them from 40d momentum helps for the same reason lagging does. Compositing cross-sectionally standardised legs is strongly additive: momentum plus kurt(15) reaches SR 2.73. Kurtosis has high SR but low IC, meaning it pays through tail names rather than broad breadth, so I want it diversified by a broad-breadth leg rather than used alone. Priority now is picking three FINAL signals that are diverse in economic content, not three near-duplicates of the same composite, since correlated picks would concentrate holdout risk.

note: Batch 6 strengthens the momentum leg by averaging neighbouring lagged-return windows and screens candidate third legs on top of the momentum plus kurtosis core
Batch 7 extends the momentum plus kurtosis plus short-vol core to four legs and tunes the short-horizon volatility and oversold-range legs
Batch 8 explores leg weighting by duplication, kurtosis-window blending for robustness, normalised short-vol variants, and five-leg extensions of the core composite
Batch 9 systematically tests rank-aggregated composites against their z-score counterparts and perturbs each leg lookback to confirm the result sits on a plateau rather than a knife edge
Batch 10 combines the averaged lagged-momentum leg with the best five-leg structures and tests skew and low-beta as an additional diversifying leg under both rank and z aggregation

text: Final selection. The signal that survived everything is a four-factor blend of cross-sectionally standardised legs: (1) LAGGED intermediate momentum, an average of delay(ret(20),10) and delay(ret(20),15), i.e. cumulative return over roughly t-35 to t-10, deliberately excluding the most recent two weeks; (2) short-window kurtosis, kurt(15); (3) low short-horizon volatility, neg(std(5)); (4) short-term reversal, neg(ret(5)). Legs 1 and 4 are economically consistent: recent returns mean-revert while the older part of the return path trends, so lagging the momentum window and shorting the last week are two expressions of the same term structure. Robustness evidence: I perturbed every leg one at a time in batches 11 and 12. Every variant landed between SR 3.23 and 3.46, so the reported numbers sit on a broad plateau rather than a peak, which is the main defence against having curve-fitted the train window. Optimal leg weights are also flat: doubling momentum and doubling kurtosis both helped by a few percent, tripling either hurt. Risk I am explicitly hedging: kurt(15) has an unusually high SR relative to its rank IC (1.74 versus 0.0048), meaning it pays through a concentrated set of tail names rather than through broad cross-sectional breadth, and its lookback profile is peaked at 15 with weaker neighbours at 10 and 20. That combination is the most likely thing to decay out of sample. I therefore spread the three reported signals across that risk rather than reporting three copies of the single best train score: pick 1 is the highest train SR with rank aggregation for bounded influence; pick 2 switches to z aggregation, averages the momentum leg over three lagged windows and adds a skew(120) leg, giving the best breadth of the three at IC 0.0177; pick 3 replaces the point estimate kurt(15) with a kurtosis leg smoothed across windows 10, 15 and 20, which costs only 0.08 of train SR and removes the dependence on one lookback being exactly right. Rejected despite good scores: variants leaning on beta or corrm legs, which had high IC but much weaker SR, and any single raw feature, since the composites roughly doubled the standalone Sharpe of their best component through diversification.

Momentum and reversal legs are two ends of the same return term structure: the recent fortnight mean-reverts while the older segment trends, which is why lagging the momentum window and shorting last week both add value. Train SR 3.38 to 3.46 with rank IC 0.016 to 0.0177. Selected for plateau stability rather than peak score: perturbing any single leg lookback one at a time kept every variant within 3.23 to 3.46, and leg weights are flat (doubling momentum and kurtosis helped slightly, tripling either hurt). The three picks deliberately spread the main decay risk, which is that kurt(15) shows a very high SR relative to its breadth (IC 0.0048 standalone) and a peaked lookback profile. Pick 1 is the top train score using rank aggregation for bounded outlier influence; pick 2 switches to z aggregation, averages momentum over three lagged windows and adds a skew(120) leg for the best breadth of the three; pick 3 smooths the kurtosis leg across windows 10, 15 and 20 so the result does not depend on one lookback being exactly right.
